variants.name: Swift structured concurrency: Task.cancel + await
variants.implementation_notes: Swift bakes both phases into the concurrency model: Task.cancel() is phase 1 (a one-way Boolean - `After the value of this property becomes true, it remains true indefinitely. There is no way to uncancel a task.`), the task observes it with Task.isCancelled/checkCancellation() at safe points or, when it is suspended in code that never checks, with withTaskCancellationHandler's onCancel closure, and awaiting the task (or the scope exit of async let/task groups) is phase 2. Structured tasks are also cancelled automatically when their scope ends. The classic flag/queue form is still justified for legacy synchronous code and for blocking calls that concurrency cannot wrap.
pitfalls: Cancellation is cooperative and carries no reason: a task that never checks (a tight non-async loop, a blocking legacy call) runs to completion even after cancel(); the cancellation handler only gives you a chance to run cleanup or unblock it.

An unstructured Task { } does not inherit cancellation from its creator: without withTaskCancellationHandler (or holding and cancelling the handle) it keeps running after the parent is stopped, which is the most common leak in Swift shutdown code.

A `try await` cleanup call inside a cancelled task throws at its first suspension point: cleanup that must run regardless belongs in onCancel or in code that is shielded from observation of the cancellation.
Never block on a semaphore or DispatchGroup on the main thread/actor while waiting for a task - the concurrency runtime may need that thread to make progress.

variants.name: GCD: queue-protected flag + DispatchGroup wait
variants.implementation_notes: Before (and alongside) Swift concurrency, the two phases were built from GCD: a serial queue or lock publishes the stop flag (phase 1), the worker loop re-checks it at safe points, performs its cleanup itself and calls group.leave() when it is done, and group.wait() (or notify(queue:)) is phase 2. This is the right binding for code that must stay compatible with older deployment targets or that wraps a blocking library call which concurrency cannot cancel.
pitfalls: Waiting on a DispatchGroup or semaphore from the main thread deadlocks or trips the watchdog: use group.notify on another queue, or await from async code.
The flag must be published through the same serial queue/lock every time it is read; a plain captured var read from another queue is a data race even if it usually works.
A worker that never reaches its safe point (a blocking call without a timeout) ignores the flag: bound the call or move it to a process you can abandon.
